headline: FBI builds replica town to simulate real-world cyberattacks, spanning 22,000 sq ft
summary: The 22,000 sq ft 'Kinetic Cyber Range' opened in February 2025, featuring fully wired houses, a hospital, and a power company to mimic a real community. It has already trained over 1,400 students from federal and local agencies.
details: The Federal Bureau of Investigation has unveiled a 22,000 square-foot replica town on its Huntsville, Alabama campus. This facility is designed to train law enforcement in simulating and investigating real-world cyberattacks.

Dubbed the Kinetic Cyber Range, the purpose-built town opened in February 2025. It features fully furnished houses, a hotel, a gas station, a grocery mart, a courthouse, a hospital, and a power company, complete with roads and traffic lights.

Each part of the town is wired with functioning devices and systems that behave as they would in a real community or business. This setup allows for hands-on training in a secure environment, preventing simulated attacks from spilling out of the facility.

Since its opening, the facility has trained more than 1,400 students, including FBI personnel and partners from other federal and local agencies. The aim is to teach investigators beyond the classroom, getting them hands-on with consumer and enterprise technologies frequently targeted by hackers.

The range also includes a data center with over 200 physical servers, running both Windows and Linux, to reflect corporate environments. This prepares investigators for responding to breaches or executing search warrants in realistic settings.

The replica town allows the FBI to simulate ransomware attacks and their real-world consequences. This includes the high-pressure decisions investigators must make when incidents could cause harm, such as hospital systems going dark.

The Kinetic Cyber Range also trains U.S. investigators in digital forensics, which involves cracking cybersecurity defenses of encrypted devices to extract data. The tools used for this are controversial as they exploit vulnerabilities not disclosed to device makers like Apple or Google.

The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report logged a record $20.9 billion in U.S. cybercrime losses, a 26% jump over the prior year. Ransomware is ranked as the top ongoing threat to critical infrastructure, highlighting the urgency of such training.
